name: Obadiah
author: The book is credited to Obadiah, whose name means 'servant of the Lord'. He was a prophet, someone who brought God's messages to the people, but nothing else is known about his family, hometown or life. Several other Old Testament figures share the name, though there is no good reason to link him with any of them.
audience: The message is addressed to Edom, a neighbouring nation descended from Esau, Jacob's brother. Its real first hearers, however, were the people of Judah, stung by the way the Edomites had looked on and joined in when Jerusalem was attacked and plundered, at a time whose exact date is still debated.
era: Most scholars connect the book to the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom sided with the invaders and took advantage of Judah's collapse. Some instead date it earlier, to around 845 BC, when Philistines and Arabs raided Jerusalem during King Jehoram's reign. Either way, Israel and Edom had a long history of bitter rivalry stretching back centuries, despite their shared ancestry.

notes.1:1: Edom's homeland lay in the rugged red-rock mountains south-east of the Dead Sea, where cliff-top settlements made its people feel safe from attack. This passage closely parallels Jeremiah 49.
notes.1:5: Later in this passage Teman is mentioned. It was a region of Edom, and Edom was famous in the ancient world for its wise men and advisers.
notes.1:10: This section is widely linked to Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC; Psalm 137 also remembers Edomites cheering the city's destruction.
notes.1:17: Later in this passage a list of places is named, spanning Israel's old lands and beyond. One of them, Sepharad, is uncertain but often identified with Sardis, a city in what is now western Turkey.

flags.problem: 'There is no good reason to link him with any of them' dismisses a long-standing traditional view. Ancient Jewish tradition (the Talmud) identified this Obadiah with the Obadiah who served King Ahab's household and hid prophets from Jezebel.
flags.suggestion: Present both views fairly, for example: 'Ancient Jewish tradition identified him with the Obadiah who served in King Ahab's household, though most scholars today think this is unlikely.'

flags.problem: This note covers 1:10–14 and the next note starts at 1:17, so verses 15–16 have no setting note. Readers on those verses will see nothing.
